case_name: Maltby, Sinclair, Perrin and Morin v. Saskatchewan Attorney General, Saskatchewan Minister of Social Services, and Director of the Saskatoon Provincial Correctional Centre
text:
Saskatchewan Court of Queen’s Bench

Judicial Centre of Saskatoon

Citation: Maltby, Sinclair, Perrin and
Morin v. Saskatchewan Attorney General, Saskatchewan Minister of Social
Services, and Director of The Saskatoon Provincial Correctional Centre

Date: 1982-11-1 and 5

Docket: 3340 A.D. 1982

Between:

Maltby, Sinclair, Perrin and Morin

and

Saskatchewan Attorney General,
Saskatchewan Minister of Social Services, and Director of The Saskatoon
Provincial Correctional Centre

Sirois, J.

Counsel:

M.P. Bodnar, for the applicants;

D.A. McKillop, for the respondents.

[
1
]

Sirois, J,: This application made pursuant to
section 24(1)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, Constitution Act 1981
, by way of Notice of
Motion on behalf of the applicants who are all remand inmates is for the
following relief:

For an order stating that the rights of the applicants as
guaranteed by the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
have been
violated by their respective treatment received as inmates of the Provincial
Correctional Centre at Saskatoon as operated by the respondents and in
particular:

(a) That the general manner in which the respondents have
detained and continue to detain the applicants as remand inmates is an
unwarranted restriction on their rights to liberty as guaranteed by
section 7

of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

(b) That the respondents’ practice of not allowing the
applicants to vote in elections is contrary to
section 3
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

(c) That the restrictions placed upon the applicants by the
respondents in the time, amount, type and area of recreational, social,
educational and work programs available to them, and the resulting daily
routine which the applicants must undergo results in their detention condition being
of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and is therefore contrary to

section 12
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

(d) That the practices of the respondents, with regard to the
use of handcuffs and leg shackles being placed upon the applicants is practised
in such a manner as to violate the applicants’ right not to be subjected to any
cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, as guaranteed by
section 12
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

(e) That the practices of the respondents with regard to strip
searches of the applicants, violates the applicants’ right to be secure against
unreasonable search and seizure as guaranteed by
section 8
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, and the right to security of the person as
guaranteed by
section 7
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,

(f) That the practices of the respondents with regard to
placing restrictions upon the location, amount, time and type of visits to the
applicants as well as restrictions placed on whom may visit the applicants
violates the applicants’ right to freedom of expression, and freedom of
association as guaranteed by
section 2
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
, and amounts to the applicants’ detention conditions being one of
cruel and unusual punishment a punishment contrary to section Freedoms.

(g) That the policy of the respondents which restricts the
number and time of phone calls, which may be placed by the applicants, as well
as prohibiting phone communication by the applicants to police forces radio or
TV stations, the Provincial Ombudsman, or newspaper offices, violates the
applicants’ right to freedom of expression and freedom of association, as
guaranteed by
section 2
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

(h) That the policy of the respondents which restricts the
availability, and form of religious practice available to the applicants is a
breach of the applicants’ rights to freedom of religion as guaranteed by

section 2
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,

[
2
]

The relevant sections of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

provides as follows:

Section 1: The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such
reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free
and democratic society.

Section 2: Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(a) freedom of conscience and religion,

(b) freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression,
including freedom of the press and other media of communication,

(c) freedom of peaceful assembly;

(d) freedom of association.

Section 3: Every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in an
election of members of the House of Commons or of a legislative assembly and to
be qualified for membership therein.

Section 7: Everyone has the right to life, liberty, and
security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in
accordance with the principles of fundamental Justice,

Section 8: Everyone has the right to be secure against
unreasonable search or seizure.

Section 9: Everyone has the right not to be arbitrarily
detained or imprisoned.

Section 12: Everyone has the right not to be subjected to any
cruel and unusual treatment or punishment .

[
3
]

The applicants are all remand inmates as opposed to inmates who have
been convicted of a crime and are serving their sentence. The remand inmates
are of course presumed to be innocent until proven guilty at their trial. The
only reasons for having them in jail are either that they were unable to post
bail, they were refused bail, to be certain that they will appear in court
whenever they are required to appear or for the protection of the public
pending their trial. While the remanded inmates are presumed to be innocent
until proven guilty, it has not been deemed wise to let them out on bail. Some
of these are charged with far more serious crimes than what the sentenced
inmates are serving. Moreover the sentenced inmates are in a ‘settled’
situation - they know where they are at - whereas the remanded inmates are
going through a period of great agitation and uncertainty and require more
supervision than the former. The status of each is vastly different and hence
different considerations apply.

[
4
]

As a rule courts uniformly refrain from considering challenges to
routine administrative assignments. Courts do not sit to superintend the
administration of the jail and penitentiary systems. What the courts do sit to
do is to Insure that those who administer that system comply with the
requirements of the Canadian Constitution. The duty to confront and resolve
constitutional questions regardless of their complexity and magnitude is the
very essence of judicial responsibility. When these arise the courts cannot
simply abdicate their function out of misplaced deference to some sort of hands
off doctrine.

[
5
]

The lawful incarceration of the applicants as remand inmates bears with
it necessarily reasonable limitations on their rights previously enjoyed in a
free and democratic society. These restrictions are no doubt the sort of
reasonable restrictions that the framers of the
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
envisioned when they included in
section 1
the words ...
“guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it
subject only to such
reasonable limits prescribed by law
...” (emphasis mine). The institution
may and certainly must place restrictions and limitations on the rights of the
applicants so that sufficient security will ensure that they will remain in
custody and will not pose a danger to themselves or to other inmates or staff.

[
6
]

. In the case of a complaint under the
Canadian Bill of Rights
, a
‘balancing approach’ in dealing with a prisoner’s complaint is utilized. Note
Solosky
v. Government of Canada
(1979),
1979 CanLII 9 (SCC)
, 30 N.R. 380, at 396. American authorities
have long used this ‘balancing approach’ in dealing with infringements of
rights guaranteed under the American Constitution. In
Bell
, Attorney
General et al. v. Wolfish et al.
October Term 1978, 441 U.S. 520, Mr. Justice Rehnquist said at p. 537: “Not every disability imposed during
pre-trial detention amounts to ‘punishment’ in the constitutional sense
however. Once the government has exercised its conceded authority to detain a
person pending trial it obviously is entitled to employ devices that are calculated
to effectuate this detention. Traditionally, this has meant confinement in a
facility which no matter how modern or how antiquated, results in restricting
the movement of a detainee in a manner in which he would not be restricted if
he simply were free to walk the streets pending trial. Whether it be called a
jail, a prison or a custodial center, the purpose of the facility is to detain.
Loss of freedom of choice and privacy are inherent incidents of confinement in
such a facility. And the fact that such detention interferes with the
detainee’s understandable desire to live as comfortably as possible and with as
little restraint as possible during confinement does not convert the conditions
or restrictions of detention into ‘punishment’.”

[
7
]

Besides ensuring that the remand inmates will remain in custody, be
present at his trial and not pose a danger to himself, other inmates and staff,
the government also has legitimate interests that stem from its need to manage
the facility in which the individual is detained. This may require
administrative measure required to maintain security and order at the
institution and make certain that no weapons or illicit drugs reach the
inmates. This is efficient management of the detention facility - a valid
objective that may justify imposition of conditions and restrictions of
pre-trial detention that are not intended as and do not Indeed constitute
punishment.

[
8
]

The applicants have several areas of complaints that are repetitive and
I intend to deal with these by category.

I. The compound for outdoor exercise. Other indoor and outdoor activity
programs.

The compound is a barren paved area surrounded on three sides by
a concrete wall approximately ten to twelve feet high at the top of which is a
large coil of razor wire; the fourth side is the wall of the remand facility
proper. This compound has an area of 5,350 square feet. Remand inmates are
provided with ball gloves, balls and footballs for use while in that area. The
compound is also used for jogging and walking. The remand inmates have access
to this compound three hours per day from Monday to Friday. On weekends it is
available for one hour in the afternoon and one hour in the evening. Besides
this, remand inmates have access to the gym complex 1 3/4 hours per day every
day from Monday to Friday. On weekends, this complex is available for a total
of 1 3/4 hours. This complex measures 6,664 square feet and facilitates indoor
sports, such as floor hockey, volleyball, basketball and badminton. Adjacent to
it is a weight lifting room which features a universal gym, an exercise bike
and a punching bag. They also have access to a games room in which is located a
billiards table, they have the use of this facility 4 1/2 hours every day of
the week. In each of the two remand units there is a television set at the
disposal of the remand inmates. Each remand unit houses approximately twelve
inmates.

[
9
]

Apart from what has already been described, remand inmates are also
provided with table games such as checkers and cards. Late movies are provided
on Friday and Saturday. Other miscellaneous activities are also provided on
long weekends on a regular basis such as card and snooker tournaments. During
Christmas season a special program is also organized. In contrast to this the
sentenced inmates have as an outdoor exercise facility a field which is
landscaped by grass with a baseball diamond, a hockey rink and a jogging trail.
This entire area is surrounded by a see-through fence, They are allowed to use
this outdoor exercising facility daily on weekdays between 6 p.m. and 8 p.m. On
weekends the hours are from 3:15 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. and also 6 p.m. to 8 p.m.

[
10
]

The average length of stay for remand inmates for the year ending March
31, 1982 for the various provincial correctional centres were:

Prince Albert

19 days

Regina

18 days

Saskatoon

26 days

Pine Grove

17 days

[
11
]

This is a relatively short period of time compared to sentenced inmates
who could be serving a sentence of anywhere up to 2 years less a day. This may
explain why the exercise facilities provided for the regular sentenced inmates
are more elaborate and extensive since they normally would spend more time
there than the remand inmates; furthermore they are also more numerous than the
others.

[
12
]

The four applicants have spent considerably more time on remand than has
the average inmate,
i.e.
32 weeks, 5 weeks, 18 weeks and 16 weeks
respectively. Unfortunately none of them chose to elaborate on the reasons for
the delays involved in having their trial. I can only surmise that some of
these delays were initiated by themselves for reasons of their own. Had the
Crown been remiss and delinquent in their duties in bringing these people up
promptly for their trial, surely the inmates would have said so. Indeed had the
Crown been too slow in getting the men to trial it would have drawn the ire of
the court for what would seem to be an intolerable length of time in custody
awaiting trial.

[
13
]

While the compound area where the remand inmates go for their outdoor
exercise may not be as elaborate as the one for the sentenced inmates - and I
have pointed out why this may well be - they are not limited to a 50 minute
period per week on a roof for outdoor exercise, as was the situation in one
jail in New York City. Neither are the remand inmates locked in their cells
some 16 hours a day as was the case in the jail cited above. In a jail in California basic standards of human decency were clearly violated when the following
conditions were discovered. The inmates confined in Greystone were locked up in
tiny, drably painted cells and confined to these cells and the society of their
cellmates, virtually 24 hours a day, seven days a week, utterly without
opportunity for recreation, exercise, vocational training, education, work or
any other activity or diversion, with the exception of those few brief periods
each week, amounting to no more than a total of two hours when they were
released to shower and shave or to visit with friends and relatives. The
heating, ventilation, plumbing and sanitation were obviously and grossly
substandard.

[
14
]

Some of the applicants deplore the lack of a rehabilitation program such
as is given to the sentenced inmates. The simple answer is that they are not in
the same category. Remand inmates are presumed to be innocent. Sentenced
inmates must face punishment, deterence and rehabilitation measures. While some
maintain that remand inmates should have access to the same rehabilitation
programs as sentenced Inmates, that position seems premature to me (since it
has not been shown that they need rehabilitation yet), and highly impractical.
What worthwhile course can you give to anyone in 26 days? The answer is clearly
none. The remand inmates admitted to such courses would be taking a free ride
with nothing at stake. They would have a disruptive influence on the sentenced
inmates whose goal is to re-establish themselves for the day when they return
to society again.

[
15
]

Looking at the entire program now in effect at the Saskatoon Correction
Institution for remand Inmates in so far as outdoor and indoor exercise and
activities are concerned, I fail to see how this could by any stretch of the
imagination constitute cruel and unusual treatment or punishment under
section
12
of the
Charter of Rights
.
There may be room for Improvement and I
understand that the matter is now under review. But at first glance it seems to
me that remand inmates have more variety in the program laid out for them then
have many of Her Majesty’s subjects walking the streets of our cities as free
men. While certain remand inmates may find the schedule of activities so
deficient that it is severely demoralizing and depressing, might I say that it
would be well nigh impossible to devise a program of activities that would meet
with the approval of all the inmates and that could be reconciled with the
purpose of the institution which is to operate a detention facility securely
and effectively. If a particular condition or restriction of pre-trial
detention is reasonably related to a legitimate government objective, it does
not, without more, amount to punishment. Conversely, if a restriction or
condition is not reasonably related to a legitimate goal - if it is arbitrary
or purposeless - a court permissibly may infer that the purpose of the
governmental action is punishment that may not constitutionally be inflicted
upon remand inmates as such.

II. The use of handcuffs and shackles.

[
16
]

Some of the applicants complain that on occasion they were taken by an
escort consisting of employees of the Provincial Correctional Centre to medical
facilities downtown in police cars with their hands handcuffed behind their
back and their legs in shackles. These inmates both swear that they have never
been charged with escaping or attempting to escape lawful custody. None of the
applicants who complained about this treatment as amounting to cruel and
unusual treatment or punishment advised the court on the extent of their
criminal record if any. This is unfortunate as it may well have shed some light
as to why the measures complained of were taken by the correctional centre. If
some of the sentenced inmates are transported without such restrictions it may
well be that they pose no security risk in the opinion of the custodial staff,
whose responsibility is to decide on such matters.

[
17
]

If there were no valid reasons for using handcuffs and shackles on a
particular case, and these were in fact used then that would or could
constitute cruel and unusual treatment or punishment contrary to
section 12
of
the
Charter of Rights
.
But simply to imply because some sentenced inmates
are escorted without handcuffs or shackles does not necessarily mean that
remand inmates are being discriminated against when these restrictions are
imposed upon them. There is no basis for concluding the remand inmates pose any
lesser security risk than convicted inmates. Indeed, it may be that in certain
circumstances they present a greater risk to jail security and order. Some
remand inmates are charged with serious crimes and have prior records. They may
also pose a greater risk of escape than convicted inmates.

[
18
]

In deciding whether or not handcuffs and/or leg bracelets should be used
the correctional centre considers:

I. the inmate’s security rating

II. inmate’s present offences with particular attention to
escapes and violence

III. inmate’s past offences with particular attention to
escapes and violence IV. inmate’s centre behaviour

V. inmate’s medical and emotional condition

VI. special circumstances

[
19
]

The restraints are routinely used to ensure safe escorts of inmates
outside secure areas of the institution and in the community. Departmental
policy is based on the belief that there is a limited requirement for the use
of physical restraint in any circumstance other than routine escort situations.
In effect it is viewed as an extraordinary security measure which should be
employed sparingly and always with care, discretion and judgment. It should in
no instance be initiated when other possible alternatives are available.
Physical restraints are never used as a form of punishment, a disciplinary sanction
or as a form of treatment for services, mental disorder or disturbance. Apart
from the use of physical restraints for escorting purposes, these are utilized
only with the approval and under the direction of designated management staff
of the facility. Only those sentenced and remand inmates with a “low security”
rating are excepted from the routinely approved forms of restraint while being
escorted.

[
20
]

Prison officials and administrators should be accorded wide ranging
deference in the adoption and execution of policies and practices that in their
judgments are needed to preserve internal order and discipline and to maintain
institutional security. Such considerations are peculiarly within the province
and professional expertise of corrections officials, and in the absence of
substantial evidence in the record to indicate that the officials have
exaggerated their response to these considerations, courts should ordinarily
defer to their expert judgment in such matters.
Bell
V.
Procunier
,
417 U.S. at 827. The unguided substitution of judicial judgment for that of the
expert prison administrators on matters such as this would to my mind be
inappropriate.

III. Strip search after visits.

[
21
]

The strip search imposed upon remand inmates after visits is objected to
as being unreasonable and against the right to security of the person contrary
to
section 7
and
8
of the
Charter
.
After all remand visits an on-duty
remand custodial worker and a C.S.T. custodial worker must strip search the
inmate before he re-enters the remand unit. This is done in the admitting area
and is part of the security requirements of the correctional centre. The
obvious reason for this requirement is to prevent and control incoming drugs,
weapons or any other control and which might pose a threat to institutional
security. If you have contact visits, and these are highly desirable, a strip
search necessarily follows. This practice of strip searches exists in all
Bureau of Prison facilities south of the border for the same reasons we conduct
ours here. They moreover have body cavity searches in the United States over and above the strip search. The latter search in the case of a male
comprises the inmate lifting his genitals and bending over to spread his
buttocks for such inspection. The inmate is not touched by security personnel
at any time during the visual search procedure.

[
22
]

In
Bell v. Wolfish
, supra, Mr. Justice Rehnquist said in part at
p. 558 et seq.: “Admittedly this practice (both strip and body cavity searches)
instinctively gives us the most pause. However assuming for present purposes
that inmates both convicted prisoners and pre-trial detainees retain some
Fourth Amendment rights upon commitment to a corrections facility, see
Lanza
v. New York
, supra,
Stroud v. United States
, 251 U.S. 15, 21 (1919),
we nonetheless conclude that these searches do not violate the Amendment, as
the Fourth Amendment prohibits only unreasonable searches,
Carroll V. United
States
, 267 U.S. 132, 147 (1925), and under the circumstances we do not
believe that these searches are unreasonable. The test of reasonableness under
the Fourth Amendment is not capable of precise definition or mechanical
application. In each case it requires a balancing of the need for the
particular search against the invasion of personal rights that the search
entails. Courts must consider the scope of the particular intrusion, the manner
in which it is conducted, the justification for initiating it and the place in
which it is conducted ... A detention facility is a unique place fraught with serious
security dangers. Smuggling of many drugs, weapons and other contraband is all
too common an occurrence ... We do not underestimate the degree to which these
searches may invade the personal privacy of inmates. Nor do we doubt, as the
District Court noted, that on occasion a security guard may conduct the search
in an abusive fashion... . Such abuse cannot be condoned. The searches must be
conducted in a reasonable manner. ... But we deal here with the question
whether visual body cavity inspections as contemplated by the M.C.C. rules can
ever be conducted on less than probable cause. Balancing the significant and
legitimate security interests of the institution against the private interest
of the inmates, we conclude that they can. ... Therefore the determination
whether these restrictions and practices constitute punishment in the
constitutional sense depends on whether they are nationally related to a
ligitimate non-punitive governmental purpose and whether they appear excessive
in relation to that purpose... . Ensuring security and order at the institution
is a permissible non-punitive objective. Whether the facility houses pre-trial
detainees, convicted inmates or both ... we think that these particular
restrictions and practices were reasonable responses by M.C.C. officials to
legitimate security concerns.”

[
23
]

I am in respectful agreement with what the learned jurist says in the
above passage. In this day and age, knowing full well the extent of the drug
scene, controls must be in effect to ensure the security of the institution and
the strip searches requested of remand inmates before they are returned to the
remand unit following a visit are no more than a minimum reasonable
requirement. Certainly no violation of the provisions of the
Charter of Rights

is involved.

IV. Visitation privileges.

Two applicants say that their visiting facility is in one of the
secure visiting rooms in the central resource area of the correctional centre.
It is a small room measuring about six feet by ten feet. It has a glassed-in
window on the front wall enabling officials who operate the maintenance to have
a clear view constantly of what occurs within the room. The two remand inmates
also complain that they have not been granted the use of the family visiting
unit.

[
24
]

One word on the Family Visiting Unit. There is only one in the entire
correctional centre. It is an apartment consisting of a kitchen, living room,
two bedrooms and a bathroom. Only sentenced inmates have access to this
facility wherein they can visit with their family in private home-like settings
for periods of up to three days. It is to assist inmates in maintaining family
relationships and reduce some of the negative inter-personal tensions resulting
from incarceration. They are intended to serve principally as a resource for
inmates serving long sentences who do not qualify for home visits with their
families. A sentenced inmate is eligible to apply for a visit in a unit after
having served 42 days of his sentence in the general population. He may apply
or re-apply for unit privileges on the 28th day after either (a) previous use
of the unit or (b) returning from temporary absence. An application is
considered only after the inmate has cleared and obtained bail on any
outstanding criminal charge. He must be a deserving inmate before his request
is considered. This is a rather new development in visiting programs for
inmates. It is only meant to be available to the more deserving inmates who are
serving long sentences. How the applicant remand inmates could ever hope to be
even considered for the occupancy of such a unit is beyond comprehension. This
is perfectly obvious at first blush when the average length of time spent at
the correctional centre by a remand inmate could not even qualify him to apply.
Furthermore their length of time at the correctional centre on the average
would not give the custodial staff sufficient time to assess their reliability
to determine whether or not they are worthy of enjoying the privilege of such a
unit.

[
25
]

Generally speaking all sentenced inmates are eligible for one 2 hour
personal visit per week, remand inmates are eligible for two 2 hour personal
visits per week as scheduled during remand unit visiting hours. A maximum of 5
visitors is allowed at one time. The visits take place in the secure visiting
room with the inmate sitting at the back of the pad facing the window. This
applies to both remand and secure inmates. Other provisions are made for
semi-secure inmates and those in normal living units. It is a matter of policy
that direct personal contact between inmates and private citizens is permitted
at the correctional centres. This is to maintain family relationships and to
provide opportunities for inmates to fulfill ongoing family responsibilities
compatible with security and administrative considerations. The Deputy Director
of Programs and the Deputy Director of Security are the officials sharing the
responsibility for the visiting programs. Each inmate submits a list of 12
family members or other persons whom they wish to visit on a regular basis by
appointment ahead of time. This list may be amended or revised on one month’s
notice. Compare this for a moment with visiting conditions as they are in some
institutions in some of the larger cities of our friendly neighbors to the
south. Visits occur in special booths under a rigorous security procedure. Each
detainee is separated from his visitor by a steel wall and a pane of bullet
proof glass 20” square. The booth is locked from behind on the detainee’s side.
These are non-contact booth visits. Voice communication for the detainee’s
booth to the facing visitor is by sound powered telephone except for a limited
number of high fidelity phones. The impact of deprivation of contact visits and
their psychological importances are real. Dr. Karl Menninger the psychiatrist
of national renown who has studied and written about prison conditions over a
long lifetime deplored non-contact visits as “the most unpleasant and most
disturbing detail in the whole prison” and. described them as “a violation of
ordinary principles of humanity”. In contrast to this, contact visits which
have prevailed in a Kansas institution for ten years without adverse
consequences were described in this way by Dr. Menninger: “I think the result
is magnificent. I mean, the prisoner has a contact with a civilised contact. He
can’t leave but he can talk, he can ask questions, he can hold a wife’s hand,
he can have the advantage of tactile and visual and auditory-re-establish
contact in all these ways and I think the result has been magnificent”. Just to
be able to touch somebody; not just to see them but just to be able to touch
them reduces tension, anxieties and frustrations.

[
26
]

Apart from these private visits, the inmates are all entitled to
business or professional visits with their lawyer and others. Any decisions of
the Deputy Director respecting visitations is subject to appeal by the inmate
for the correctional centre Director. Inmates are advised of their appeal
options and the procedure to be followed. The decision of the correction centre
Director is subject to a further review by the Provincial Ombudsman.
Considering the average length of time that remand inmates are kept at the
correctional centre, these visiting privileges while they may be restricted for
security reasons do not in my estimation come close to being cruel and unusual
treatment or punishment contrary to
section 12
or a breach to the inmate’s
right to freedom of expression and association as described in
section 2
of the

Charter
.
Rather, I see reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be
demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society as stated in
section 1

of the
Charter.

[
27
]

I do not agree with the applicants’ position that they should be able to
see who they want, when they want and do whatever they want with a visitor. The
restrictions imposed are incidental to another legitimate government purpose,
i.e.

security, rather than punishment. In determining whether restrictions are
reasonably related to the Government’s interest in maintaining security and
order and operating the institution in a manageable fashion, courts must heed
that such considerations are particularly within the province and professional
expertise of corrections officials, and in the absence of substantial evidence
in the record to indicate that the officials have exaggerated their response to
these considerations, courts should ordinarily defer to their expert judgment
in these matters.

V. Telephone calls and mail procedures.

The applicant, Maltby complains that he has been restricted to
one personal telephone call per day of 15 minute duration. Moreover he
complains that he was prevented from telephoning the Press and the office of
the Provincial Ombudsman. The applicant Sinclair also complained that he had
been denied requests to telephone the office of the Provincial Ombudsman on
numerous occasions. Both say that this amounts to violation of their right of
freedom of expression and freedom of association as guaranteed by
section 2
of
the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

[
28
]

The operational procedure for remand inmates with respect to telephone
calls is that an inmate is allowed one personal phone call per day and as many
business calls as they need. The staff place the call for the inmate and
confirm that it is the correct party; if the person wishes to speak to the
inmate concerned, the call is transferred to the inmate. Calls are to be kept
at a 20 minutes maximum between the hours of 7 a.m. and 10 p.m. Long distance
calls are collect.

[
29
]

I am at a loss to understand what would be gained by telephoning the
press except to create more havoc and confusion. The men are going to have
their day in court; their cases are not going to be tried in newspapers or by
newspapermen whose major aim is to create sensationalism to increase their
circulation. That is not the way things are done in this country. It may well
be that when the matter does come up in court that an order will be granted
prohibiting publication of the proceedings or any part thereof until trial so
as to better protect the accused’s interests, inter alia.

[
30
]

The operational procedure with respect to mall is as follows. Incoming
mail is picked up at the reception desk by on-duty staff members and the mail
is opened by the staff in front of the inmate. Money, cheques, personal effects
or contraband is removed by the staff, whatever the inmate may not keep will be
taken by the staff. The inmate will be given a receipt and the staff member
will initial the envelope. Outgoing mail is given to the staff members who
delivers it to the reception area. All out-going mail must have a name and
return address. The staff must not open Government, lawyer or mail from the
Ombudsman. Neither should anyone on staff open any mail going to the Ombudsman.

[
31
]

The applicants’ affidavits do not disclose the reasons for wanting to
call the Ombudsman. There is no mention of unusual restraint being used in
their material. This official has in the past investigated complaints of cruel
and unusual punishment and he has in instances recommended that this type of
conduct be prohibited by the department. It involved the use of certain kinds
of restraints in some instances where these were used not to protect an inmate
from himself or to protect others from him but for other reasons.

[
32
]

The Ombudsman over two years ago recommended that:

1. the practice of taping and gagging inmates be terminated
immediately regardless of the reasons for doing so.

2. That the use of restraints of any kind be limited to those
situations where restraints are essential to preventing Inmates from either
harming themselves or others, and only until medical assistance can be
obtained,
i.e.
that the use of restraints be prohibited where they are
utilized to reduce noise or to stop unacceptable social behavior, etc.

3. That medical advice be immediately obtained whenever,
restraints are used, and that a medical report be provided to the Director or
Acting Director within 24 hours of restraints being used.

4. That restraints not be used until the approval of the
Deputy Director, Security or the Acting Deputy Director. Security is obtained
and that every incident involving the application of restraints be the subject
of a report to the Director or the Acting Director within 24 hours of the time
the use of restraints was approved.

5. That sufficient psychiatric and medical services be
available at each correctional centre to ensure that immediate resort to these
services can be made as soon as an Inmate is identified by nursing and the
staff as being or appears to be becoming unmanageable.

[
33
]

These recommendations were accepted by the department officials, acted
upon and followed by correctional officers since that time, which coincides
with the opening of the new correctional centres in Saskatoon and Prince Albert at a cost of some $25,000,000.00. I understand that the Ombudsman is
continuing to monitor the situation.

[
34
]

I am satisfied that the applicants could well have contacted the
Ombudsman either by telephone or by mail had they wanted to, so their rights
have not been violated in the manner in which they suggest. They have simply
been subjected to reasonable limits under the circumstances.

VI. Religions practices.

[
35
]

The applicants contend that their condition of incarceration has
resulted in an infringement of their right of freedom of religion as guaranteed
by
section 2
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.
One
applicant complains that his repeated requests to attend weekly chapel services
at the Provincial Correctional Centre have been denied to him. In May he says
he was allowed to see a priest of his faith, Roman Catholic, only after six
days of continuous requests made to employees of the Provincial Correction
Centre. He believes that thus his right to freedom of religion as guaranteed by
section 2 of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
has been
infringed. Another applicant claims he has repeatedly been denied his requests
to see a Protestant chaplain. Another applicant of native origin says he is an
active adherent to native religious practice. Only recently was he allowed by the
prison officials to have access to an Elder on an irregular basis for the
purpose of conducting religious ceremonies only in the remand games-room.
Because it contains a pool table and because of its small size this inmate
believes the facility to be inadequate for the proper practice of his religion.
Thus he believes that his right to freedom of religion as guaranteed by the
Charter

is being infringed. His affidavit was sworn on the 16th of September. Yet on
the 18th of July the same inmate wrote to the Director in the following terms:

Sir:

I write this letter on behalf of the inmates, especially
myself, of secure. We wish to thank you for your extraordinary cooperation, and
the cooperation of your staff, in making our religious ceremonies possible this
weekend. Without your full cooperation the past weeks efforts and ceremony
would never have been a reality.

I would also express my gratitude in your willingness to meet
with myself when I so requested.

In allowing this past weeks events to take place you have
shown my people your appreciation of our heritage, and religious beliefs.

In closing I express my utmost respect to your abilities of
being an excellent and fair administrator.

Again, I thank you.

(signed) Ivan Morin

Inmate Secure Unit.

The religious program in the correctional centre is as follows.
A chaplain works in the centre nearly everyday. Church services for inmates
living in the normal living units are given in the chapel every Sunday morning.
Inmates who wish to attend simply have to notify their corrections workers on
the Saturday. Church services for inmates in the remand and security units are
held in their units. Other kinds of services or religious groups may be
arranged by telling the chaplain what you would like and it can be done. If an
inmate wants a private visit with the chaplain, he can make the request with
the corrections worker and the latter will make arrangements for this. The
chaplain can see you either in his office or in the unit. If an inmate wishes
to see a certain minister in particular from outside, he can make the request
to the chaplain who will try to have him come to see the inmate. If an inmate
wishes the chaplain to visit with himself and his family, he can make the
request either to the chaplain or to his corrections workers and this will be
planned.

[
36
]

The reason why all inmates do not have access to the chapel service is
again one of security. The sentenced inmates in the normal living units have
the highest security rating and they alone are accorded this privilege. To
enable a number of others from remand, secure and semi-secure units to attend
the church service proved not to be practical from an administrative or
security point of view. I do not see why an inmate cannot Include a clergyman
on his list of people that he wishes to see and telephone him directly. There
is nothing in the program that prohibits this sort of request in any way. It is
easy to see why an inmate may have problems contacting a particular clergyman.
These people of the cloth are becoming a rare commodity indeed and they are
torn asunder by demands from everywhere in the community. To blame the
correctional centre for delays in seeing a priest is simply not being
realistic. Likewise to criticize the adequacy of a certain room for the practice
of a particular religion leaves me somewhat skeptical, especially when the
inmate has written the director praising him for his efforts in this regard a
few months ago. In the armed forces you have two church parades - one Roman
Catholic and one Protestant and the men go to the one of their choice. Even
then, you still have some who claim allegiance to the Jewish, Mohammedan or
other religions in an effort to escape church parade altogether. Those
practices are not condoned - all have to go to church and worship as they
please.

[
37
]

It seems to me that the religious programs at the corrections centre,
although not perfect allow for freedom of conscience and religion within such
reasonable limits as are feasible under the circumstances. I see no
infringement of
section 2
of the
Charter
on this ground.

VII. The right to vote.

On the 26th of April an applicant made a request on his behalf
as well as on behalf of other eligible remanded inmates to an officer of the
Provincial Correctional Centre that they be taken to a polling booth for the
purpose of voting in the provincial election. This request was refused. Thus
the applicant believes that his right to vote as guaranteed by
section 3
of the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
has been violated.

[
38
]

Section 3 says: Every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in an
election of members of the House of Commons or of a legislative assembly and to
be qualified for membership therein.

[
39
]

Under section 27 of the
Elections Act
, R.S.S. 1978, vol. III
prisoners in jail or persons undergoing punishment for a criminal offence on
the day of the issue of the writ, at any time after the issue of the writ and
prior to polling day, or on polling day are disqualified to be registered as
voters and shall not vote. Clearly remand inmates are not disqualified from
voting under the
Provincial Elections Act.
Some of the remanded inmates
including the applicant may have been disqualified from voting in this election
for some other reason, such as being away from where he ordinarily resided on the
day on which the writ was issued, or was not 18 years of age, or had not
ordinarily resided in Saskatchewan for six months preceding the day on which
the writ was issued. It would not be practical or reasonable for instance to
haul an inmate from Saskatoon to Estevan to vote if that is where he is
entitled to vote. Under these circumstances were he outside the correctional
centre he would not vote in any event. There is no mechanism in the
Elections
Act
providing for inmates to vote in an election. This is a matter that
should be looked into by the legislators, by the Chief Electoral Officer and
others who are responsible for administering the
Act.
A mechanism could
possibly be set up similar to that used for hospitals and sanatoriums under
section 90 of the
Act.
In any event as the statute now stands recourse
for voting provisions should be sought elsewhere then with correctional centre
officials. Moreover simply because remanded inmates retain certain
consitutional rights does not mean that these rights are not subject to
restrictions and limitations. Lawful incarceration brings about the necessary
withdrawal or limitation of many privileges and rights, a retraction justified
by the considerations underlying our penal system. The fact of confinement as well
as the legitimate goals and policies of the penal institution limits
incidentally perhaps but necessarily some constitutional rights. There must be
a mutual accommodation between institutional needs and objectives and the
provisions of the Constitution that are of general application. This principle
applied equally to remanded as well as sentenced inmates. A person in custody
simply does not possess the full range of freedoms of an un-incarcerated
individual. The maintaining of institutional security and preserving internal
order and discipline as essential goals that may require limitation or
retraction of the retained constitutional rights of both remanded and sentenced
inmates. The problems that arise in the day-to-day operation of a corrections
facility are not susceptible of easy solutions. Prison administrators therefore
should be accorded wide ranging deference in the adaption and execution of
policies and practices that in their judgment are needed to preserve internal
order and discipline and to maintain institutional security. Rights and
freedoms in the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
are guaranteed
subject only however to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be
demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society, (section 1 of the
Constitution
Act, 1981 Part 1 Schedule B Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms).
The
facilities in Saskatoon and Prince Albert were opened and have been in use for
going on two years now. Constructed on the module plan they are a tremendous
step forward in the treatment of inmates. One might feel quite justifiably that
these institutions look more like a hospital than a prison. But the corrections
people are still not satisfied that they have reached the ultimate in custodial
care particularly with regard to remanded inmates. A Remand Review has been
formally undertaken; it is hoped that an interim report should be completed by
the 30th of November of this year and the final report by the 1st day of
February of next year. Hopefully this review will pave the way for further
improvements in the living conditions of remanded inmates while awaiting their
day in court.

[
40
]

It was Winston Churchill while he was Home Secretary of Great Britain
who observed with characteristic eloquence that “the mood and temper of the
public in regard to the treatment of crime and criminals is one of the most
unfailing tests of the civilization of any country”.

[
41
]

The order sought by the applicant under
section 24(1)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
is refused. Their rights have not been
violated by the treatment received as remanded inmates.

ADDENDUM TO JUDGMENT DATED NOVEMBER 1ST, A.D. 1982 -- Sirois,
J.

[
42
]

The closing paragraph of my reasons for judgment bearing the above date
reads as follows:

The order sought by the applicants under
section 24(1)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
is refused. Their rights have not been
violated by the treatment received as remanded inmates.

Upon due reflection and consideration the said paragraph should
be amended as follows: The order sought by the applicants under
section 24(1)

of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
is refused except with
respect to the relief sought in paragraph (b) of the notice of motion which
reads as follows:

(b) That the respondents’ practise of not allowing the
applicants to vote in elections is contrary to
section 3
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
;

As the
Election Act
now reads, remand inmates are not
disqualified from voting; the only inmates who are disqualified are prisoners
in jail or prison undergoing punishment for a criminal offence. Provision is
not made in the statute for a mechanism similar to that set up for hospitals
and sanitoria under s. 90 of the
Act
for them to vote. While recourse
cannot be had by the applicants to correction centre officials to assist them
in their right to vote, recourse can certainly be had to the other named
respondents who are elected representatives of the people in the legislature
and Ministers of the Crown. To the extent that the statute makes no exception
in their case, their rights as guaranteed by
section 3
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
to my mind have been violated. So the order
sought is allowed to that extent but refused on all other grounds.

Application allowed in part.
